# Filelayer

> A Node library that puts a single authorization decision point in front of file storage for multi-tenant applications. Public files and private files share one model. Files live in S3/R2, on a local filesystem, or in memory; all metadata, grants and audit events live in your own Postgres. Not a hosted service, not a CDN, not an image pipeline.

> **It is authorization middleware, not row-level security.** It decides for calls made through it, in your application process. The schema additionally refuses cross-tenant grants, cross-project identities and delegation amplification from *any* writer, including a `psql` session — those are constraints and triggers. But there is no RLS policy in `schema.sql`, and a direct `SELECT` against these tables is not filtered by anything: `SELECT * FROM file` returns every tenant's rows. If you write SQL against this schema instead of calling the library, no authorization runs and no audit event is written. Filelayer composes with database-level enforcement; it does not replace it.

Status: alpha / developer preview, version 0.20.0, Apache-2.0. Never deployed in production. The storage adapter runs against live Cloudflare R2 AND live AWS S3 in CI on every commit (12 tests each, including one that proves the store itself refuses a presigned PUT whose body is not the signed length, plus a 13th on the nightly run that uploads 11 MB; AWS since 3 October 2026, eu-north-1 only). The schema may change in any 0.x release. Requires Node >= 22.18. Install: `npm install @filelayer/core`.

Freshness: this file describes version 0.20.0 and was written on 2026-10-07. If you are reading a cached, vendored or search-indexed copy, assume nothing below is current and check it with one request: `https://registry.npmjs.org/@filelayer/core/latest` returns the current version as JSON, and it cannot be stale. If that version is not 0.20.0, every figure below is from an earlier release and you should re-fetch https://filelayer.dev/llms.txt before relying on any of it. This warning is here because the absence of it has already cost us: in October 2026 an evaluator that had been given only cached pages declined Filelayer and quoted, as a current fact, our own sentence saying the storage adapter had never run against real AWS. The sentence was true when we wrote it and false when it was read, and nothing in the copy that evaluator held said which.

This file is for an agent writing an integration. It is ordered by what you need to get right, not by what is interesting.

Every link below points at GitHub. If you are reading this out of an install you may have neither network nor browser, and you do not need them: the same files are on disk under `node_modules/@filelayer/core/` — `README.md`, `docs/QUICKSTART.md`, `docs/guides/`, `llms.txt` (this file), `openapi.json`, `schema.sql`, `SEMANTICS.md`, `MIGRATIONS.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `LICENSE`, `NOTICE`, plus `src/`, `test/`, `examples/` and `migrations/`. Three resolve as subpath imports: `@filelayer/core/llms.txt`, `@filelayer/core/openapi.json`, `@filelayer/core/schema.sql`. The copies are byte-identical to the ones GitHub shows; a repository check fails the build if they diverge.

## Start here

- [README](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/README.md): what it is, the alpha banner, the five security properties, and the Limitations list. Read Limitations before you design around a capability.
- [QUICKSTART](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/docs/QUICKSTART.md): install to first file, then each tier, then the three configuration steps for a real deployment.
- [SEMANTICS](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/packages/core/SEMANTICS.md): the exact behaviour of every edge — liveness, delegation and attenuation, deletion, the audit chain, redirect delivery. This is the reference to consult when a test surprises you.

## The API you will actually call

Everything is an in-process method call. There is no REST API to call over the network.

- Entry point: `import { Filelayer } from '@filelayer/core'`. Throwaway instance: `await Filelayer.quickstart({ baseUrl })` (PGlite + in-memory bytes, everything lost on exit). Real instance: `new Filelayer(pgPool, storage, { baseUrl })` where `storage` is one of three adapters — `new FsStorage('./data')` for bytes on a local disk (no bucket, no IAM user, survives a restart, no `presignGet` so redirect delivery is unavailable), `new S3Storage({ endpoint, bucket, region, accessKeyId, secretAccessKey })` for S3 or R2, or `new MemoryStorage()` which dies with the process. If you have a disk and no bucket, `FsStorage` is the answer; it exists because an agent in your position wrote one by hand from the type definitions.
- **`npm install @filelayer/core` installs no runtime dependencies.** `quickstart()` and `createTestDb()` additionally need `@electric-sql/pglite`, an *optional peer dependency* — `npm install --save-dev "@electric-sql/pglite@^0.3.11"`. Keep the version constraint: the supported line is **0.3.x**, 0.5.x is not supported (the suite does not pass against it), and PGlite's `latest` on npm is 0.5.x, so a bare install can pick a version outside the declared peer range and npm refuses the tree with `ERESOLVE`. Nothing else needs it; a production instance takes your own `pg.Pool`. If you call them without it, the thrown error names the package and the exact command.
- Tiered facade, keyed on your own identifiers: `fl.files` (`put`, `get`, `list`, `stat`, `delete`, `publish`, `unpublish`, `publicUrl`), `fl.orgs` (`create`, `setRole`, `removeMember`, `audit`, `verifyAudit`), `fl.shares` (`create`, `revoke`, `unshare`, `list`, `redeem`), `fl.ids` (`actorId`, `orgId`, `ensureActor`).
- **Your own ids reach the whole API, including the HTTP routes.** `fl.files.list({ as, org, capability, limit, cursor })` is the listing screen. `deliveryHandler(fl, { principal: (req) => ({ as: yourUserId(req) }) })` is the authenticated read route: return `{ as }` with YOUR user id, or `{ as: null }` for an anonymous caller. An `as` this project has never seen is a 404 and the attempt is audited, never a downgrade to anonymous. Both landed in 0.13.0; before it the route required an internal uuid that no public call returned, so it could not be mounted by an application with its own user ids. `fl.ids.actorId(external)` / `fl.ids.orgId(external)` return the internal uuid or null and create nothing; `fl.ids.ensureActor(external)` creates if absent and is idempotent, unlike the core `fl.createActor()` which is a bare insert and throws on a second call.
- Full surface, keyed on internal ids and an explicit `Principal`: `fl.upload`, `fl.read`, `fl.readStream`, `fl.stat`, `fl.share`, `fl.revoke`, `fl.listGrants`, `fl.redeem`, `fl.redeemStream`, `fl.auditLog`, `fl.verifyAuditChain`, `fl.addMember`, `fl.removeMember`, `fl.delete`, `fl.collectStorageOrphans`, and -- only when `directUpload` is configured with the verbatim `DIRECT_UPLOAD_ACKNOWLEDGEMENT` -- `fl.createUpload`, `fl.completeUpload`, `fl.collectUploadReservations`.
- **The audit log answers in your identifiers, not internal uuids.** Every row from `fl.orgs.audit()` / `fl.auditLog()` carries the uuids it always did (`actorId`, `fileId`, `orgId`) *and* a resolved view: `row.actor.label`/`.externalId`, `row.file.label`/`.name`, `row.org.label`/`.externalId`, plus `row.summary` — one printable line, e.g. `2026-09-06T10:12:41.002Z marco file.read deny:grant_revoked contract.pdf @acme`. `label` is never null: an access with no principal reads `anonymous`, an event with no tenant reads `system`, and an id that resolves to nothing in your project keeps its uuid and says `resolution: 'unresolved'`. Resolution is project-scoped and costs no extra query.
- [simple.ts](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/packages/core/src/simple.ts): the facade, with the option types. No authorization logic lives here.
- [filelayer.ts](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/packages/core/src/filelayer.ts): the full surface and every signature.
- [index.ts](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/packages/core/src/index.ts): the complete export list. If it is not exported there, it is not public API.

## Things that will bite you if you assume otherwise

- **This project's documents are written for you, and that is a deliberate choice with a cost.** Every claim on a public surface is checked by a gate: version stamps, test counts, live-storage counts, that every documented code sample runs, that every path inside the tarball resolves inside the tarball, and that every migration file produces the schema it claims. The reason is that an inaccurate document wastes an implementer's time and ours, and an agent reading to write an integration has no way to tell a stale number from a fresh one. The cost, pointed out by a human reader on 5 October 2026 and fairly: stars, issues and design partners come from people, and a README written as a specification reads as fear. So the README now leads with what the thing does and this file carries the premise -- which is where it belonged.
- **Which schema version a database is at is readable off the database, and applying migrations is YOUR job.** `schema.sql` creates `filelayer_schema_version` and stamps it as its last statement, and since 0.15.0 it REFUSES a database that already has the schema -- on its first statement, naming the version it found -- rather than dying part-way on `relation "project" already exists`. `schemaStatus(db)` returns `{ state, at, expects, outstanding, history }` where `state` is `current | behind | ahead | unversioned | absent`; for a database created before 0.15.0 it infers the version and names the object the inference rests on, so you can check it. **It issues no DDL and never will**: there is no migration runner here and there is not going to be one, because your application already owns one. The forward SQL is one file per change under `node_modules/@filelayer/core/migrations/`, each with a single runnable path and a guard that refuses if the database is not in the state it expects; `migrations/manifest.json` is machine-readable and carries `transactional` (false where the file needs `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, which Postgres refuses inside a transaction) and `requiresDecision`. CI applies each file to the previous release's schema and fails the build unless the result matches the next release's, on real PostgreSQL. Entries 1 and 2 have no file: they predate the oldest tag, so there is no earlier schema to apply them to, and that is stated rather than hidden.
- **`shares.create` IS NOT IDEMPOTENT, and a grant id is not a person's access.** Every call inserts a grant row. Two calls for the same file and the same recipient leave TWO live grants, which doubles an effective `maxDownloads` and -- the part that matters -- means `shares.revoke(grantId)` on the id you were handed last leaves the earlier grant live while reporting success. The recipient keeps reading. Use **`shares.unshare(fileId, { as, user })`** to remove a named user's access: it revokes every live grant naming them, in one transaction, and is idempotent. Use `revoke(grantId)` only for a share LINK whose secret you handed out. Found in 0.10.0 by giving an integration task to an agent that had only the published tarball; fixed in 0.11.0.
- **There is no `public` boolean.** `put(bytes, { public: true })` creates an anonymous *grant row*, identical to `share({ subject: { type: 'anonymous' } })`. `unpublish()` revokes it. Do not look for a column; there is not one and there will not be one.
- **A public URL is served by your own process, not by a CDN.** `publicUrl(id)` returns `<baseUrl>/f/<id>`, which is re-authorized on every request. That is why revocation is immediate, and it is also why the default path proxies every byte. The two facts are the same fact.
- **`as:` naming an unknown identity is a 404, not an anonymous read.** There is no silent downgrade. A typo in a user id denies; it does not quietly become a public read.
- **Denials are 404, not 403,** for anything that would confirm a file exists — including revoked, expired and exhausted grants. The true reason is in the audit log, not in the response. Do not branch on 403 to detect "exists but forbidden". **Lacking a capability is also a 404**: an org member who calls `orgs.setRole` or `orgs.audit` without being an admin gets `404 insufficient_role`, the same answer a stranger gets. 403 is narrower than that: it is for a caller who DOES hold the capability and is asking for something the rules forbid anyway — `role_escalation`, `superior_target`, `last_owner`, and the delegation refusals `attenuation_violation` and `subject_breadth_amplification`. If you are rendering "you need admin rights", branch on your own session, because this API will not tell you.
- **Writes auto-provision an identity only in an org the SAME CALL creates.** `put({ owner })` with no `org:`, or with an `org:` that does not exist yet, registers that user as a `member` of it. `put({ org: 'existing', owner: 'newcomer' })` is **`403 no_membership`** -- it does not quietly add somebody to a tenant that already has members. Call `orgs.setRole(org, user, role, { as: admin })` first. This changed in 0.6.0 and this line said the opposite until 0.12.0; measured against the published 0.11.0. Reads never auto-provision at all.
- **Identifiers are unique per project, not per org.** `actor.external_id` and `org.external_id` are scoped to a project. Two orgs in one project cannot both have a user called `alice` *meaning different people* — the id resolves to one actor for the whole project. One actor being a member of many orgs is fine and normal (`membership` is keyed on `(org_id, actor_id)`); two different humans sharing an id is what is impossible.
- **A share LINK carries `read` and nothing else.** `shares.create(id, { as, capabilities })` with any other capability throws `FilelayerError(400, 'link_is_read_only')` before any query, and `grant_link_read_only` in the schema refuses the row even from `psql`. To delegate `delete` or `share`, name an actor or an org as the subject; a bearer link travels through mail clients and chat logs, and anything beyond `read` on one turns a disclosure into a destruction.
- **A share secret is returned exactly once.** Only its SHA-256 is stored. If you do not persist or deliver it at creation time, it is unrecoverable.
- **Delegated shares are attenuated, and the clamp is silent-but-visible.** `share()` returns the *effective* `expiresAt` and `maxDownloads`, which may be tighter than what you asked for. Read the returned values; do not assume you got what you requested.
- **Org admins and owners can read `private` files.** Deliberate. If you must exclude the operator you need envelope encryption, which does not exist here.
- **`collectStorageOrphans()` is a job you must schedule.** Bytes are written before metadata commits, so a crash in between leaves an unreferenced object. Nothing calls it for you.
- **`deliveryHandler` is `node:http` and CANNOT be mounted in a Next.js App Router, Hono, a Worker, Deno or Bun.** It takes `(req, res)` and writes to a `ServerResponse`; those runtimes hand you a `Request` and want a `Response` back. Since 0.20.0, `deliveryFetch(fl, { principal })` is the same two routes for them, with the same `Range` parsing, the same 416 carrying the object's size, the same refusal of a credential in the query string and the same 401 that tells a client to retry a password link as a POST. It returns `null` for a request it does not own, so a catch-all route does not swallow the rest of the application. Two things it will not do: it does not read `X-Forwarded-For` (a `Request` has no socket and that header is written by whoever spoke last, so on a directly reachable deployment it is the client choosing what its own audit log says -- pass `clientIp` if you sit behind an edge you trust), and it does not set `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'`, which is your file and without which Next may serve a previously authorized response to a later caller. [examples/nextjs](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/examples/nextjs/README.md) is upload, list, read, share and revoke in four files, driven by CI on every commit against a freshly packed tarball.
- **You can check YOUR OWN integration, not just ours.** `auditIntegration({ owner, stranger, app })` takes four callbacks written against your routes and verifies the properties against your running application: the owner reads their own file; a stranger is refused 404 rather than 403, because a 403 confirms the file exists; an anonymous caller is refused; an id your application has never seen DENIES rather than degrading to anonymous; `nosniff` and `attachment` are on the bytes; the response is not publicly cacheable; byte ranges are answered correctly, including the invalid range that must be IGNORED and the unsatisfiable one that must carry the size; and revocation lands on the next request. It imports none of your code and knows nothing about your framework. A pass means those properties held for the requests it made, which is not a security audit; a failure is a request that got an answer it should not have. The harness is itself verified against eleven deliberately broken applications, each with exactly one property wrong. Since 0.20.0. Everything else runnable in this project checks US -- the suite, the starter's verify.mjs, the guide proofs -- and none of it answers whether your application is correct.
- **Every error code is enumerated, typed and machine-readable.** `FilelayerError.code` is a union of the 29 codes this library can produce, not `string`, so a `switch` over it is exhaustive and a typo is a compile error. THE STATUS IS A FUNCTION OF THE CODE: one code never means two statuses, and the constructor does not accept a status at all -- it reads it from the catalogue in `src/errors.ts`. The full list with what to do about each is [ERRORS.md](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/packages/core/ERRORS.md), and the machine-readable form is [errors.json](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/packages/core/errors.json), which ships in the tarball and resolves as `@filelayer/core/errors.json`. Both are GENERATED from the code and a gate fails the build if they drift, in either direction: a code thrown and not catalogued, or catalogued and unreachable. Do not serialize `e.reason` to an untrusted caller: it carries the internal deny reason and would be an enumeration oracle. `e.code` is the safe field. Since 0.20.0; before it `code` was `string` and the published tables named eight of the twenty-nine.
- **The shipped HTTP routes answer `Range`.** `fileDownloadRoute()` and `shareDownloadRoute()` parse the header and return 206 with `Content-Range`; `Accept-Ranges: bytes` is on every proxied response, including the unranged 200, which is the response a client actually reads to decide whether it can seek. A range past the end is 416 with `Content-Range: bytes */<size>` — not 404, which is what it used to be. The status is derived from the headers, not a parameter, so a partial body can never go out as a 200. Three edges, all deliberate: multiple ranges in one request are ignored and the whole object is served (answering one of several under a 206 cannot be distinguished by the client from an answer to a different question); `If-Range` is not parsed, which is safe only because an object key is a fresh UUID that is never rewritten; and a range is dropped when a download cap binds, with `Accept-Ranges: none` to say so, because charging per seek would make `maxDownloads: 3` mean "three seeks".
- **`fl.files.put()` takes a `Uint8Array`** and is therefore fully resident in memory. Use `fl.upload()` with a `ReadableStream` above a few tens of megabytes.

## Serving bytes over HTTP

- [openapi.yaml](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/openapi.yaml) / [openapi.json](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/openapi.json): the complete HTTP surface. It is two routes: `GET /f/{fileId}` and `GET|POST /d/{secret}`. There are no others, and no upload, share or admin endpoints exist over HTTP.
- [delivery.ts](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/packages/core/src/delivery.ts): `deliveryHandler(fl)` is both routes plus a 404, as one `node:http` listener. `deliveryFetch(fl, opts)` is the same two routes as one `(Request) => Promise<Response | null>`, for Next.js App Router, Hono, Workers, Deno and Bun. `toResponse` / `toStreamResponse` build a `Response` when you want to assemble it yourself; `sendNodeResponse` / `sendNodeStream` for `node:http`.
- **Use the writers.** `read()` and `redeem()` return bytes *plus* the exact headers required to serve them safely. Writing `res.writeHead(200, { 'content-type': f.contentType })` re-opens stored XSS in your own origin; `res.writeHead(200, f.headers)` does not. The headers cannot be disabled.
- **Never put a password in a query string.** BOTH byte routes refuse one: `/d/{secret}` with 400 `credential_in_query`, `/f/{fileId}` with 400 `credential_in_query_string`. The refused keys, matched case-insensitively, are `password`, `pw`, `pass`, `passwd`, `token`, `secret` and `key`. A password-protected link answers 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: FilelayerShare`; retry as POST with the password in the body.

## Data model and operations

- [schema.sql](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/packages/core/schema.sql): the data model. Every security property is commented at the constraint that enforces it. Resolvable from an install at `node_modules/@filelayer/core/schema.sql`, or via the exported `SCHEMA_PATH` and `loadSchemaSql()`.
- [authz.ts](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/packages/core/src/authz.ts): the decision engine. Two functions, one core. `toPublicError()` is the deny-reason to HTTP-status mapping.
- [MIGRATIONS](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/packages/core/MIGRATIONS.md): how schema changes are delivered, with a numbered entry per break. §2a is the one to read if you are upgrading rather than installing.
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/packages/core/CHANGELOG.md): the real history, including security defects found internally.

## Guides

Answers to questions people actually ask, written to be useful whether or not you use this library. The code in them is executed by `npm run check:docs` on every commit, and where a guide states a number, a script beside it reproduces that number against a real PostgreSQL. Index: [docs/guides/](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/docs/guides/README.md).

- [Expiring and revocable file links](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/docs/guides/expiring-and-revocable-file-links.md): why a presigned URL cannot be revoked, the four things you can do instead, and the one query that is easy to write wrong — with the schema and the SQL to copy. Read this before designing any share feature on presigned URLs.
- [Private file uploads](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/docs/guides/private-file-uploads.md): a presigned PUT does not limit the size of the body — a URL issued for a 200 KB avatar accepts three gigabytes — and the presigned POST policy that does. Plus the content-type trap, why the object key is not access control, and why the upload happening outside your transaction leaves orphans. NOTE: as of 0.10.0 Filelayer DOES do pre-authorized direct upload via `createUpload()`/`completeUpload()`, opt-in behind `DIRECT_UPLOAD_ACKNOWLEDGEMENT`. Only S3 and R2 keep your server out of the data path; `FsStorage` with an `upload` block does work, for development, and reports `via: 'server'` because the bytes go through your process there. It signs `content-length` and `content-type` into the presigned PUT, which closes the size hole the guide describes; it does not use presigned POST, because R2 does not implement it.
- [Multi-tenant file access control](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/docs/guides/multi-tenant-file-access.md): Row-Level Security filters which rows a session may READ and does not stop it WRITING a grant that joins two tenants — demonstrated, and refused by a composite foreign key that holds even against a role with BYPASSRLS. Plus why the bytes in your bucket are outside every policy you wrote.
- [Deleting files and orphaned objects](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/docs/guides/deleting-files-and-orphaned-objects.md): delete the ROW first, because an orphaned object is a recoverable failure and a row pointing at nothing is not. Then the part nobody writes down: the sweeper that reclaims orphans deletes on the strength of an ABSENCE, and a partial listing is indistinguishable from one. Measured — the same short listing hides orphans in a storage-driven sweep and destroys live rows in a DB-driven one.

## Runnable references

- [tier1-avatar](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/examples/tier1-avatar/app.ts): a public avatar.
- [tier2-user-files](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/examples/tier2-user-files/app.ts): private, user-owned files.
- [tier3-org-roles](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/examples/tier3-org-roles/app.ts): multi-tenant with roles.
- [vault](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/examples/vault/server.ts): a full B2B document workspace over HTTP.
- [starter](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/examples/starter/server.ts): the deployable one — your own Postgres, `FsStorage` by default, the schema applied once under an advisory lock, and the route helpers mounted beside routes of your own. `verify.mjs` next to it drives the whole thing over HTTP in 24 checks, and CI boots the starter against a real PostgreSQL and runs them on every push, so the example is tested rather than merely published. Start here if you are standing an application up rather than reading one.
- [test/](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/tree/main/packages/core/test): the property suite. It ships inside the npm tarball, so the behaviour claimed above is checkable from what you installed. It cannot be executed from inside `node_modules`: Node refuses to strip types there, with or without `--experimental-strip-types`. Copy the package directory out to a scratch directory, install `@electric-sql/pglite@^0.3.11`, and run `node --test 'test/*.test.ts'`. Zero failures, no server and no credentials, about two minutes; a handful skip because they need two real database connections, and the exact tally to expect is in the document below. The exact commands are in [docs/VERIFY-WHAT-YOU-INSTALLED.md](https://github.com/filelayer/filelayer/blob/main/docs/VERIFY-WHAT-YOU-INSTALLED.md), which ships beside the tests, and CI runs that document's commands verbatim against a freshly packed tarball on every commit. Do NOT clone the repository to run the suite: that verifies our checkout rather than the bytes you were sent, which is the only thing worth verifying here.
